chapters.title: Chapter 2: Computing a Company's Taxable Income

lessons.title: From Accounting Profit to Taxable Income: Why the Two Numbers Differ

body.text: Your profit and loss account answers to accounting standards and to your shareholders. Your tax computation answers to the Income-tax Act. They start from the same business, use the same invoices, and arrive at two different numbers. Neither one is wrong.

children.text: Every year, a company's auditor signs off on a profit figure, and then the same company files a return showing a different one. Founders often assume something has gone wrong, or that the accountant is doing something clever. Neither is true. The tax law simply refuses to accept some expenses your accountant correctly recorded, insists on its own depreciation numbers, and waits for cash to actually move before allowing certain deductions.

The document that reconciles the two is called the computation of income. Learning to read it is the single most useful tax skill a business owner can pick up, because every rupee of difference is a rupee of tax you either pay or save.

body.latex: \text{Taxable income} = \text{Profit before tax} + \text{Disallowed items} - \text{Extra deductions the law allows}

body.title: Quick Check: Which One Survives?
body.question: Four items appear in a company's profit and loss account. Which one is fully deductible when computing taxable income?
options: ₹2,00,000 penalty paid to a pollution control board for exceeding limits
₹2,00,000 of salaries paid to factory workers, with TDS deducted and deposited on time
₹2,00,000 provision for a warranty claim that may arise next year
₹2,00,000 of CSR spending on a village school, as required by the Companies Act
body.explanation: Salaries are ordinary business expenditure under section 34 [old 37(1)], and deducting TDS on time keeps them safe from the disallowance in section 35 [old 40]. A penalty for breaking a law is never deductible. A provision is an estimate, not an incurred cost. CSR spending is mandatory under company law but is specifically not treated as business expenditure, which surprises a lot of founders.

children.text: Gone Forever, or Just Gone This Year?
Not all add-backs hurt equally. Some deductions are lost permanently. Others are only postponed, and come back to you in a later year. Knowing which is which changes how you react.

columns.label: Permanent: the deduction never comes back
points: Penalties and fines for breaking a law
CSR spending required under the Companies Act
Personal expenses routed through the business
Income tax and the surcharge and cess on it
Manage these by not incurring them, because tax planning cannot rescue them

columns.label: Timing: the deduction is only postponed
points: GST, PF and other statutory dues paid after the year end
Dues to micro and small suppliers paid late
Expenses where TDS was deducted and deposited in a later year
The gap between book depreciation and tax depreciation
Manage these with cash flow and discipline, because the money is only stuck, not lost

body.text: Timing differences are exactly what the deferred tax line on your balance sheet is measuring. When tax depreciation runs ahead of book depreciation, the company pays less tax now and more later, and accounting records that future obligation as a deferred tax liability. Nobody is hiding anything. It is the bridge in this lesson, written in accounting language.

body.title: Try It: Build the Bridge
body.prompt: A Ludhiana garment exporter reports book profit of ₹80,00,000. Its books carry depreciation of ₹6,00,000, and it paid a ₹1,50,000 penalty for a labour law violation. Depreciation under section 33 [old 32] works out to ₹9,00,000. What is its taxable income? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: Start at ₹80,00,000. Add back book depreciation of ₹6,00,000 and the non-deductible penalty of ₹1,50,000, taking you to ₹87,50,000. Then deduct tax depreciation of ₹9,00,000, leaving ₹78,50,000, or ₹78.5 lakh. Here taxable income is below book profit, because tax depreciation exceeded book depreciation by more than the disallowance.

children.text: The Add-Back That Catches Small Businesses

Section 37 [old 43B] carries one rule that has caused more unpleasant March conversations than any other in recent years. Amounts owed to micro and small enterprises registered under the MSMED Act are deductible only in the year they are actually paid, and only if paid within the agreed period, capped at 45 days, or within 15 days where there is no written agreement.

body.title: Scenario: The Supplier Who Waited
body.scenario: A Rajkot engineering firm buys ₹40,00,000 of components during the year from a supplier registered as a micro enterprise. Its standard payment terms with everyone are 90 days. As on 31 March, ₹9,00,000 of these invoices are unpaid and are past the 45-day window. The firm's book profit is ₹50,00,000 and it is in the 22% regime.
body.prompt: What happens to the ₹9,00,000, and what should the firm do differently next year?
body.modelAnswer: The ₹9,00,000 is added back under section 37(2)(g) [old 43B(h)], so taxable income becomes ₹59,00,000 rather than ₹50,00,000. At 25.168%, that is roughly ₹2,26,512 of extra tax this year, on a cost the firm genuinely incurred. The deduction is not lost forever: it becomes available in the year the supplier is actually paid, so this is a timing difference that hurts cash flow now and reverses later. Two fixes matter. First, identify which suppliers are registered micro or small enterprises, since the rule depends on their registration status and not on their size as you perceive it. Ask for their Udyam registration number and tag them in the accounting system. Second, change payment terms for those suppliers to 45 days or less, because a blanket 90-day policy is exactly what triggers this. A March review of unpaid MSME dues, with the clearly overdue ones settled before the year closes, avoids the add-back entirely.

body.text: Statutory dues follow a gentler version of the same rule. GST, provident fund, ESI and similar dues outstanding at the year end are still deductible if you pay them before the due date for filing your return under section 263 [old 139]. Miss that date and the deduction shifts to whichever year you eventually pay in. Dues to micro and small suppliers are stricter: the payment deadline is the one in the MSMED Act, not your filing date.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Estimates and Actuals
body.textWithBlank: A provision for doubtful debts is not deductible, because tax law allows the deduction only when the debt is actually ___ off in the books.
body.explanation: Accounting is cautious and books an expected loss early. Tax law waits for the loss to become real. The same logic explains why provisions for warranties, gratuity estimates and similar figures get added back, while the actual payment or write-off is allowed in the year it happens.

body.title: Questions to Ask Your Accountant Before the Return Is Filed
steps: Show me the computation of income next to the profit and loss account, and walk me down the add-backs
Which of these add-backs are permanent, and which reverse in a later year?
What are we losing this year because TDS was not deducted or deposited on time?
How much do we owe micro and small suppliers past the deadline right now, and can we clear it before 31 March?
Are any statutory dues unpaid, and will they be paid before the return filing date?
How far apart are book depreciation and tax depreciation, and why?
What is our effective tax rate on book profit, and does the gap from 25.17% make sense?

body.title: Where the other heads of income come in

children.text: A company's profit and loss account often contains income that the tax law does not treat as business income at all. Rent from a let-out building falls under income from house property. Interest on fixed deposits and most dividends fall under income from other sources. Profit on selling land or a building falls under capital gains.

In a full computation, each of those is removed from business profit and added back under its own head, where its own rules on deductions and rates apply. Total income is then the sum of all heads. For most small and mid-sized businesses, with revenue coming from one trade, this step is short. For a company sitting on property or a large treasury book, it matters a great deal.

cards.definition: The statement that bridges audited book profit to taxable income, listing every add-back and deduction.
The general rule allowing expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the business, if it is not capital or personal in nature.
Amounts that cannot be deducted, including expenses where TDS was not handled correctly and partner remuneration above the ceiling in 35(e).
Deductions allowed only on actual payment, covering statutory dues, bonus, bank interest and dues to micro and small suppliers under 37(2)(g).
An add-back that never becomes deductible, such as a penalty or CSR spending.
An add-back that reverses in a later year, such as unpaid statutory dues or the gap between book and tax depreciation.
The accounting entry that records tax effects of timing differences, so the books show the tax a company will eventually pay.

points: Book profit and taxable income are different by design, and the computation of income is the document that reconciles them
Expenses get disallowed for four reasons: the law refuses them, it wants proof of payment, a condition was broken, or it measures the item differently
Penalties, CSR spending and personal expenses are permanent losses, while unpaid dues and depreciation gaps are only postponed
Section 37(2)(g) [old 43B(h)] disallows dues to micro and small suppliers until they are actually paid, making 45-day payment terms a tax decision
Book depreciation is always added back and replaced by depreciation computed under section 33 [old 32]
The gap between your effective tax rate and the headline 25.17% is explained entirely by these adjustments
